sequence.name: The Island
sequence.text:
1
The Island
10 MINUTES
Instructions

NOTE: The Island is a spreadsheet you make yourself with one column called Island and another column called Canoed Away.

If a question is still mystifying after Camo, just add the citation of the question to the Island.

This means at least one of these three things is true:

I don't understand why the right answer is right.

I don't understand why the wrong answer is wrong.

I have no idea how I could get this right in the future.

At the start of prep each day, spend 5 minutes on the Island retrying a question or two. 

If the question clicks, move it to Canoed Away. Otherwise, keep it on the Island. 

Fill in your Wrong Answer Journal with the new information you've learned now that the question has canoed away.

Click here to go to The Island (scroll to the bottom!)

Thunderdome
30 MINUTES
Instructions

NOTE: Thunderdomes are advanced workouts for those who have plateaued. Beginners can make good progress with other workouts before attempting a Thunderdome.

For each stimulus in the section*, write or speak out each and every one of the following outputs, according to the stimulus type, without looking at the question stem or answer choices:

On an Argument, write or speak your own:

Weaken correct answer

Strengthen correct answer

Necessary assumption

Sufficient assumption

Method correct answer

Argument parts identifications

Parallel Skeleton

Parallel correct answer

Use your favorite topic as a consistent analogous base

This means all your Parallel correct answers can be about dogs or cars across all the questions in the section.

On a Debate, write or speak your own:

Controversy

Agreement

Loophole in both speakers

On a Paradox, write or speak your own:

Resolution

Inference

Contradiction

On a Premise Set, write or speak your own:

Three Inferences

Contradiction

sequence.name: Translation + CLIR Drill
sequence.text:
3
Translation + CLIR Drill
1 SECTION
Instructions

Start a stopwatch.

Read and translate the stimulus* out loud in chunks.

Quip each chunk of the stimulus after you translate.

Continue this process on every stimulus chunk until you reach the end of stimulus.

Immediately proceed to the CLIR after your final quip of the stimulus (or the final quip is the CLIR).

Stop the stopwatch and record your time.

sequence.name: Test-Day Timing Marathon
sequence.text:
4
Test-Day Timing Marathon
8 SECTIONS
Instructions

Complete six to eight test-day timed LR sections* in one sitting with no breaks, or complete six to eight test-day timed RC sections in one sitting with no breaks.

This means you should use test-day timing on all sections, not Marathon timing.

Immediately proceed to the next section in the Marathon as soon as the test-day timer expires.

Any questions left unanswered within time will be marked wrong.

NOTE: You can modify the Test-Day Timing Marathon to alternate between LR and RC sections, as you would in a Mixed Section Marathon. Just flip a coin (or ask your favorite digital assistant to flip a coin) to decide each section when you're ready to begin that section mid-Marathon.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.name: Camo Review
sequence.text:
5
Camo Review
Instructions

When you finish an LR or RC section in LawHub, do not press Complete Section. Instead, write down your answers.

Use Self-Paced Mode on all LR and RC sections. Never use Exam Mode.

At least 24 hours later, enter your answers into Camo Review.

Do not check your answers against the answer key before entering your answers into Camo Review.

Camo Review will give you a list of questions to return to.

This list includes all of your wrong answers and an unknown number of decoy correct answers.

Reattempt all of the questions in your Camo Review from scratch. Attempt to do a better job on the question now than you did the first time.

Doing a better job means you should retranslate, requip, and re-CLIR the stimulus on LR or retranslate and requip the passage on RC. Retranslate every part of the question, consider every answer choice, and try to correct your process mistakes before choosing a new answer.

Enter all your new answers into Camo Review.

Camo Review will identify all your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, Self-Doubt, and Self-Confidence answers.

Your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, and Self-Doubt answers have been automatically added to your Wrong Answer Journal. Go to your Wrong Answer Journal now to immediately begin the Wrong Answer Journal process.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.name: Wrong Answer Journal
sequence.text:
6
Wrong Answer Journal
Instructions

After you've Camoed your LR or RC section, begin the Wrong Answer Journaling process.

For each wrong answer, fill in the date you did the section, the question number that was wrong, and the answer you chose.

This information will already be filled in for you if you Camo using Loophole Online.

Fill in your Reason Missed column

In this column, write down what you did wrong that caused you to miss this question.

Example: "I misidentified the question stem."

This will force you to reflect on what you did that caused you to choose the wrong answer and overlook the right answer.

In this column, write down what you will do differently to ensure you don't make this same mistake again.

Ask yourself, "What could I have done that would have made me realize in the moment that the wrong answer is wrong? What could I have done that would have made me realize in the moment that the right answer is right?"

The first words of every entry in this column should be "I will..." 

Example: "I will do Question Stem Training to improve my ability to correctly identify question types."

Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines are the best way to push yourself to improve stamina and test-day readiness at the same time.

The first few sections of a Test-Day Timing Marathon may be rocky, but you should gradually acclimate to how a test-day timed section feels.

Don't attempt Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines if your Marathon-timed sections are 10+ minutes from test-day timing. Test-Day Timing Marathons are more appropriate when you're within 5 minutes of test-day timing.

Test-Day Timing Marathons don't allow for natural time progression in the same way Marathon Routines do, so they risk compromising your accuracy and process far more than the other Speed Routines.

How This Should Be Done

To maximize the value of Test-Day Timing Marathons, treat this Routine just like test day (except for no breaks after section 2 😅).

This Routine is basically test day on steroids. If you can get your goal section-level accuracy in this Routine, you are already getting ahead on our Perform Prep Stage goals.

Marathon Routine Protocols

Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

SHOW LESS
How to Move On

If your Test-Day Timing Marathons crash and burn even though you've seen goal time and accuracy on Marathon-timed sections before, you may just be anxious about the countdown timer and need experience to acclimate.

Mixed Timing Marathon Routines are the best remedy for that situation because they ground you in your accurate, controlled process between test-day timed sections.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in your Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine, take a Practice Test (PT).

sequence.text:

The Island
10 MINUTES
Instructions

NOTE: The Island is a spreadsheet you make yourself with one column called Island and another column called Canoed Away.

If a question is still mystifying after Camo, just add the citation of the question to the Island.

This means at least one of these three things is true:

I don't understand why the right answer is right.

I don't understand why the wrong answer is wrong.

I have no idea how I could get this right in the future.

At the start of prep each day, spend 5 minutes on the Island retrying a question or two. 

If the question clicks, move it to Canoed Away. Otherwise, keep it on the Island. 

Fill in your Wrong Answer Journal with the new information you've learned now that the question has canoed away.

4
Test-Day Timing Marathon
8 SECTIONS
Instructions

Complete six to eight test-day timed LR sections* in one sitting with no breaks, or complete six to eight test-day timed RC sections in one sitting with no breaks.

This means you should use test-day timing on all sections, not Marathon timing.

Immediately proceed to the next section in the Marathon as soon as the test-day timer expires.

Any questions left unanswered within time will be marked wrong.

NOTE: You can modify the Test-Day Timing Marathon to alternate between LR and RC sections, as you would in a Mixed Section Marathon. Just flip a coin (or ask your favorite digital assistant to flip a coin) to decide each section when you're ready to begin that section mid-Marathon.

sequence.name: Camo Review
sequence.text:
5
Camo Review
Instructions

When you finish an LR or RC section in LawHub, do not press Complete Section. Instead, write down your answers.

Use Self-Paced Mode on all LR and RC sections. Never use Exam Mode.

At least 24 hours later, enter your answers into Camo Review.

Do not check your answers against the answer key before entering your answers into Camo Review.

Camo Review will give you a list of questions to return to.

This list includes all of your wrong answers and an unknown number of decoy correct answers.

Reattempt all of the questions in your Camo Review from scratch. Attempt to do a better job on the question now than you did the first time.

Doing a better job means you should retranslate, requip, and re-CLIR the stimulus on LR or retranslate and requip the passage on RC. Retranslate every part of the question, consider every answer choice, and try to correct your process mistakes before choosing a new answer.

Enter all your new answers into Camo Review.

Camo Review will identify all your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, Self-Doubt, and Self-Confidence answers.

Your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, and Self-Doubt answers have been automatically added to your Wrong Answer Journal. Go to your Wrong Answer Journal now to immediately begin the Wrong Answer Journal process.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine
  1. Prep Map/

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine

Why are we doing this?

Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines are the best way to push yourself to improve stamina and test-day readiness at the same time.

The first few sections of a Test-Day Timing Marathon may be rocky, but you should gradually acclimate to how a test-day timed section feels.

Don't attempt Test-Day Timing Marathon Routines if your Marathon-timed sections are 10+ minutes from test-day timing. Test-Day Timing Marathons are more appropriate when you're within 5 minutes of test-day timing.

Test-Day Timing Marathons don't allow for natural time progression in the same way Marathon Routines do, so they risk compromising your accuracy and process far more than the other Speed Routines.

RC

Do these workouts in this order. For real, the order matters.

How to Pull This Off

To maximize the value of Test-Day Timing Marathons, treat this Routine just like test day (except for no breaks after section 2 😅).

This Routine is basically test day on steroids. If you can get your goal section-level accuracy in this Routine, you are already getting ahead on our Perform Prep Stage goals.

Marathon Routine Protocols

  • Warm up before any Marathon-style Routine so you can hit the first section with a running start.

    • If you don't warm up first, the Marathon will not speed you up as much because it will take you longer to build momentum.

  • Always Camo + Wrong Answer Journal at the end of a Marathon Routine day to avoid building up too much Camo debt.

    • The normal "wait at least 24 hours before you Camo" rule does not apply to Marathons.

  • Never interrupt a Marathon to Camo in between sections.

  • Camo the Marathon sections in the order of completion.

    • This means you should Camo the first section of your Marathon first, the second section next, and so on.

  • Complete the entire Camo + Wrong Answer Journal process for each Marathon section before checking any Marathon scores and before starting the Camo process on another Marathon section. Camo and Wrong Answer Journal each section one at a time.

How to move on

If your Test-Day Timing Marathons crash and burn even though you've seen goal time and accuracy on Marathon-timed sections before, you may just be anxious about the countdown timer and need experience to acclimate.

Mixed Timing Marathon Routines are the best remedy for that situation because they ground you in your accurate, controlled process between test-day timed sections.

If you're hitting your goal time and accuracy in your Test-Day Timing Marathon Routine, take a Practice Test (PT).

sequence.name: Answer Choice Warmup
sequence.text:
1
Answer Choice Warmup
Instructions

Open up a previously-seen LR or RC section*.

Translate the first four questions' answer choices in the style of a Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet.

Read only the answer choices for these four questions.

Do not read the stimulus or the question stem.

Write down each individual answer choice.

Write down a Translation of each answer choice.

This means read A, write the literal text of A, and write the Translation of A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E.

Use the same spreadsheet and same style as you used when you completed the Answer Choice Translation Primer.

Translate the next four questions' answer choices in the style of an Out Loud Answer Choice Translation Drill.

Read only the answer choices in the section.

Do not read the stimulus.

Do not read the question stem.

Translate the answer choice out loud.

Quip the answer choice out loud.

This means read A, translate A, and quip A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E.
SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

Answer Choice Warmup

Instructions

  1. Open up a previously-seen LR or RC section*.

  2. Translate the first four questions' answer choices in the style of a Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet.

    1. Read only the answer choices for these four questions.

      1. Do not read the stimulus or the question stem.

    2. Write down each individual answer choice.

    3. Write down a Translation of each answer choice.

      1. This means read A, write the literal text of A, and write the Translation of A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E.

    4. Use the same spreadsheet and same style as you used when you completed the Answer Choice Translation Primer.

  3. Translate the next four questions' answer choices in the style of an Out Loud Answer Choice Translation Drill.

    1. Read only the answer choices in the section.

      1. Do not read the stimulus.

      2. Do not read the question stem.

    2. Translate the answer choice out loud.

    3. Quip the answer choice out loud.

sequence.name: Mini-Cycle
sequence.text:
2
Mini-Cycle
1 SECTION
Instructions

NOTE: Mini-Cycles involve working through full LR sections in batches of 9 questions at a time, without breaks between batches. Do not do less than a full section*.

For questions #1-3, translate and CLIR the stimulus only.

Do not look at the question stem or answer choices yet.

For questions #4-6, Party Trick the answer choices only.

Do not read the stimulus yet.

For questions #7-9, complete the full question according to the straight-through LR Full Question Process.

Return to questions #1-3 and Party Trick them.

After Party Tricking #1-3, relook at the stimulus and change your answer if needed.

Return to questions #4-6 and translate and CLIR.

Choose an answer based on your new understanding of the stimulus.

Note if the answer choice differs from your original Party-Tricked choice.

Repeat this process with the next 9 questions, and then again with the remaining questions in the section. It’s expected that the last batch of questions is less than 9, so you won’t do as many full questions in that batch.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

Instructions

Complete the section* according to your typical process, but make one small adjustment.

You are allowed to choose E as a correct answer. You just can't read answer E before you choose it.

You may read answer E on the hyperskip pass.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS
Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

This Routine purposefully messes with the answer choices to get you to wake up and stop auto-piloting your way through them.

We have some Answer Choice Translation in the warmup and some Party Tricking in the Mini-Cycle. But since the E Blackout removes one of the answers, it forces you to individually evaluate each answer choice's unique relation to the stimulus rather than acting comparatively and choosing the "best" answer. 

There's always just one right answer, and its correctness is determined by its individual relationship to the stimulus, not its relationship to any other answer choice.

This Routine is built to break down these bad answer choice habits.

How This Should Be Done

Students are often desperate to break a plateau, but they aren't desperate to change their habits.

Take the answer choice disruption in this Routine as an opportunity to get you out of any funks you've been in.

This Routine is designed to make you re-examine the answer choices you've taken for granted.

Don't be put off by the uncertainty inherent in the E Blackout or in Party Tricking in the Mini-Cycle. This level of uncertainty is a gift to help you build your intuition.

How to Move On

This is a good Routine to return to intermittently when your answer choices start to get sloppy.

There's no need to move on from it permanently since it can be useful even in the week of your test to offer an answer choice tune-up.

sequence.name: Answer Choice Warmup
sequence.text:
1
Answer Choice Warmup
Instructions

Open up a previously-seen LR or RC section*.

Translate the first four questions' answer choices in the style of a Written Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet.

Read only the answer choices for these four questions.

Do not read the stimulus or the question stem.

Write down each individual answer choice.

Write down a Translation of each answer choice.

This means read A, write the literal text of A, and write the Translation of A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E.

Use the same spreadsheet and same style as you used when you completed the Answer Choice Translation Primer.

Translate the next four questions' answer choices in the style of an Out Loud Answer Choice Translation Drill.

Read only the answer choices in the section.

Do not read the stimulus.

Do not read the question stem.

Translate the answer choice out loud.

Quip the answer choice out loud.

This means read A, translate A, and quip A. Then repeat the same process on B, C, D, and E.
SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.name: Mini-Cycle
sequence.text:
2
Mini-Cycle
1 SECTION
Instructions

NOTE: Mini-Cycles involve working through full LR sections in batches of 9 questions at a time, without breaks between batches. Do not do less than a full section*.

For questions #1-3, translate and CLIR the stimulus only.

Do not look at the question stem or answer choices yet.

For questions #4-6, Party Trick the answer choices only.

Do not read the stimulus yet.

For questions #7-9, complete the full question according to the straight-through LR Full Question Process.

Return to questions #1-3 and Party Trick them.

After Party Tricking #1-3, relook at the stimulus and change your answer if needed.

Return to questions #4-6 and translate and CLIR.

Choose an answer based on your new understanding of the stimulus.

Note if the answer choice differs from your original Party-Tricked choice.

Repeat this process with the next 9 questions, and then again with the remaining questions in the section. It’s expected that the last batch of questions is less than 9, so you won’t do as many full questions in that batch.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

Question Stem Training
3+ SECTIONS
Instructions

Identify all the LR question stem types and their associated Back Up Plans in a section*.

Your wrong question stem identification

How you could know the correct identification next time

sequence.name: Unofficial Diagramming Marathon
sequence.text:
4
Unofficial Diagramming Marathon
Instructions

Look back at your most recently used LR sections to identify the questions that allow an opportunity for diagramming.

Reattempt these questions with a new mindset, one that embraces diagramming as a useful tool.

Try diagramming a few borderline stimuli, even if you aren't sure they should be diagrammed.

This is how you learn the line between where diagramming is helpful and where it's not helpful.

The Unofficial Diagramming Marathon only ends when you no longer feel any hesitation to diagram, there is no fear of diagramming left, and diagramming seems boring and rote.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

This is a great Intro LR Routine to improve conditional diagramming skills.

How This Should Be Done

The star of this Routine is the Unofficial Diagramming Marathon, so definitely prioritize it in how you structure your time during this Routine.

If you're new to the Accuracy Prep Stage when you start this Routine, you can use your old Translation + CLIR sections for the Unofficial Diagramming Marathon. If you've never seen the answer choices on these sections, don't spoil them during the Unofficial Diagramming Marathon. Just stick to the stimuli when you look for opportunities to diagram.

If you have plenty of question-answering sections to review in the Unofficial Diagramming Marathon, that's great! Make sure to look at both the stimuli and the answer choices for opportunities to diagram on those.

How to Move On

You can move on when you no longer feel any hesitation or doubt in diagramming a conditional statement. And I mean that literally. Zero hesitation. And zero doubt. 

If you need to do this Routine more than once to hit that standard, that's totally fine. Just keep on going with this Routine until you hit the standard.

sequence.name: Caffeinated RC Translation Drill
sequence.text:
1
Caffeinated RC Translation Drill
1 PASSAGE
Instructions

Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

Take a few seconds to confirm your Translation with the paragraph you just read.

In this step, you are not rereading from scratch. 

You're confirming the Translation you already have is right. 

This style of confirming your Translation with the text applies to every confirmation you ever do on RC.

Repeat this pattern for all remaining paragraphs.

At the end of the passage, confirm your Translation with the entire passage. This should take 15-30 seconds.

OPTIONAL: Look away and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of the entire passage silently.

This step is optional, but you should do it when you first begin Caffeinated RC Translation Drills and periodically afterward, just to confirm that you can.

Complete this same process on all remaining passages in the section.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

1

Caffeinated RC Translation Drill

1 passage

Instructions

  1. Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

  2. Take a few seconds to confirm your Translation with the paragraph you just read.

    2. You're confirming the Translation you already have is right. 

    3. This style of confirming your Translation with the text applies to every confirmation you ever do on RC.

  3. Repeat this pattern for all remaining paragraphs.

Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

Thunderdomes and Pacing Practice go well together because Thunderdomes give you depth, breadth, and agility while Pacing Practice keeps you moving. For maintaining accuracy, it's helpful to mix Workouts that naturally run at different paces. If you always go fast, you can start to get sloppy and the accuracy drops. If you always go slow, you'll get distracted and lazy, which will also cause the accuracy to drop. This Routine Progression balances those tendencies.

How This Should Be Done

Approach this Routine like contrast therapy. Each workout exercises two distinct LSAT skillsets, so you want to put your full attention into growing your skills as much as you can in each Workout, even though you aren't getting a score on the Thunderdome.

You can switch the Thunderdome between LR and RC. Ideally, you're completing a full section of the Thunderdome, but I wouldn't do less than 10 Thunderdome questions at a time in this Routine, since you're completing ~50 questions in the Pacing Practice sections, you don't want the Thunderdome practice to be imbalanced.

How to Move On

If the Pacing Practice is working to reduce the time gradually while building accuracy with the Thunderdome, move to The Fast and Slow Routine 2 after you feel comfortable taking on the challenge of completing each Thunderdome output within 30 seconds. The Pacing Practice should help with this goal.

If the Pacing Practice is not reducing time as quickly as you would like, you can always switch the Pacing Practice to Light Failsafes or just move to the Speed Core Routines. They will bring the time down more dramatically.

If you're within two weeks of your target test date, you shouldn't spend too long on this Routine. It works as a way to introduce you to the timed environment, while still building accuracy skills with the Thunderdome, but you'll need the blunt force of Marathon Routines to bring the section time down by your test date.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

inline_prep.name: Stop Oversimplifying
inline_prep.text:
Accuracy
FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
Prep Map
/
Accuracy
TELL ELLEN
FIX 2 OF 7
Stop Oversimplifying
What Problem Are We Solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

sequence.name: Caffeinated RC Translation Drill
sequence.text:
1
Caffeinated RC Translation Drill
1 PASSAGE
Instructions

Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

Take a few seconds to confirm your Translation with the paragraph you just read.

In this step, you are not rereading from scratch. 

You're confirming the Translation you already have is right. 

This style of confirming your Translation with the text applies to every confirmation you ever do on RC.

Repeat this pattern for all remaining paragraphs.

At the end of the passage, confirm your Translation with the entire passage. This should take 15-30 seconds.

OPTIONAL: Look away and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of the entire passage silently.

This step is optional, but you should do it when you first begin Caffeinated RC Translation Drills and periodically afterward, just to confirm that you can.

Complete this same process on all remaining passages in the section.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.name: Pacing Practice
sequence.text:
2
Pacing Practice
1 SECTION
Instructions

Choose an interval time goal.

Your interval time goal is your target time for each question.

For example, an interval time goal may be 90 seconds per question.

Follow the procedures of How to Set a Realistic Interval Time Goal below.

Set an interval timer to repeatedly countdown from that time goal 30 times in a row.

Do not incorporate rest intervals.

We choose 30 times so we can have some extra intervals in case our timer messes up.

Start your interval timer when you begin an LR or RC section*.

For RC, only use the interval timer on the questions, not during the passage.

You must select an answer on each question before the interval timer goes off.

You cannot stay on a question longer than the interval timer permits, no matter how badly you want to.
SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.text:
4
HIIT (High Intensity Interval Training)
Instructions

NOTE: Do not attempt HIIT if you have never done a Thunderdome. Ideally, you've done several Thunderdomes and begun to feel confident while Thunderdoming before ever attempting HIIT.

After you finish your Translation + CLIR on a given stimulus at 20-minute pace, complete the stimulus' Thunderdome without looking at the stimulus again*.

Cap each Thunderdome output at 30 seconds outloud.

Use AI voice dictation to record your Thunderdome outputs while keeping the workout speedy. My favorite dictation software is Flow; it's free up to 2000 words per week.

If you go over 30 seconds per Thunderdome output, don't worry about it. Just aiming for 30 seconds will make you faster.

Why Are We Doing This?

The combination of HIIT and Pacing Practice unify the skillsets built in The Fast and Slow Routine I. HIIT takes the depth, breadth, and agility from the Thunderdome and applies the Pacing Practice mechanic to allow you to bridge your comprehensive mastery towards test conditions.

Don't let yourself get out of your flow between the Pacing Practice and HIIT. Go straight between the Workouts, almost like a Marathon. The combination of Workouts should create a really cool flow state by the end.

If the Pacing Practice is not working as quickly as you would like, you can always switch the Pacing Practice for Light Failsafes or just move to the Speed Core Routines. This will bring the time down more dramatically.

If you're within two weeks of your target test date, you shouldn't spend too long on this Routine exclusively. This Routine can work well on an every other day pattern with the Speed Core Routines or with PTs though.

1

Caffeinated RC Translation Drill

1 passage

Instructions

  1. Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

  2. Take a few seconds to confirm your Translation with the paragraph you just read.

    1. In this step, you are not rereading from scratch. 

    2. You're confirming the Translation you already have is right. 

    3. This style of confirming your Translation with the text applies to every confirmation you ever do on RC.

  3. Repeat this pattern for all remaining paragraphs.

  4. At the end of the passage, confirm your Translation with the entire passage. This should take 15-30 seconds.

  5. OPTIONAL: Look away and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of the entire passage silently.

    1. This step is optional, but you should do it when you first begin Caffeinated RC Translation Drills and periodically afterward, just to confirm that you can.

  6. Complete this same process on all remaining passages in the section.

sequence.text:

Pacing Practice
1 SECTION
Instructions

Choose an interval time goal.

Your interval time goal is your target time for each question.

For example, an interval time goal may be 90 seconds per question.

Follow the procedures of How to Set a Realistic Interval Time Goal below.

Set an interval timer to repeatedly countdown from that time goal 30 times in a row.

Do not incorporate rest intervals.

We choose 30 times so we can have some extra intervals in case our timer messes up.

Start your interval timer when you begin an LR or RC section*.

For RC, only use the interval timer on the questions, not during the passage.

You must select an answer on each question before the interval timer goes off.

You cannot stay on a question longer than the interval timer permits, no matter how badly you want to.

HIIT (High Intensity Interval Training)
Instructions

NOTE: Do not attempt HIIT if you have never done a Thunderdome. Ideally, you've done several Thunderdomes and begun to feel confident while Thunderdoming before ever attempting HIIT.

After you finish your Translation + CLIR on a given stimulus at 20-minute pace, complete the stimulus' Thunderdome without looking at the stimulus again*.

Cap each Thunderdome output at 30 seconds outloud.

Use AI voice dictation to record your Thunderdome outputs while keeping the workout speedy. My favorite dictation software is Flow; it's free up to 2000 words per week.

If you go over 30 seconds per Thunderdome output, don't worry about it. Just aiming for 30 seconds will make you faster.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Oversimplifying
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Oversimplifying

What problem are we solving?

There is no such thing as "just a detail" on the LSAT. 

Ignoring "details" leads to missing question through oversimplifying. If you run with an inaccurate, oversimplified version of the text, you're bound to miss questions.

Answers are right and wrong based on "just one word." That doesn't make the LSAT mean, evil, or unfair. It makes the LSAT a test of precision.

And precision is something you'd to have when you're a lawyer, right? You don't want to be the attorney who harms their client because you missed "just one word." 

Every word on the LSAT deserves equal levels of respect, as it works with every other word to create a conceptual Translation of each sentence.

Conceptual Translation can be the single biggest differentiator between high and lower scorers. It is the opposite of oversimplifying. When you ignore some words in an answer choice and focus solely on other words (keywording), you're not conceptually translating that answer. You're oversimplifying and massively increasing your risk of missing the question.

Keywording reduces an answer's fate solely to whether it has certain words from the stimulus.

However, there are many correct answers that contain no words from the stimulus. There are many wrong answers that contain tons of words from the stimulus. 

You cannot oversimplify answer choice selection to a shallow matching game and expect the LSAT to tolerate it. It won't. 

But this is just one way oversimplification decreases your score. There are approximately one million other ways oversimplification decreases your score. 

This Accuracy Fix trains you to embrace complexity because your mind is strong enough to handle it. Luckily, this is something you were trained to do in the Translation Prep Stage. Now is the time to put that training into action, especially in the answer choices. 

That's how we stop you from missing so many questions.

HIIT (High Intensity Interval Training)
Instructions

NOTE: Do not attempt HIIT if you have never done a Thunderdome. Ideally, you've done several Thunderdomes and begun to feel confident while Thunderdoming before ever attempting HIIT.

After you finish your Translation + CLIR on a given stimulus at 20-minute pace, complete the stimulus' Thunderdome without looking at the stimulus again*.

Cap each Thunderdome output at 30 seconds outloud.

Use AI voice dictation to record your Thunderdome outputs while keeping the workout speedy. My favorite dictation software is Flow; it's free up to 2000 words per week.

If you go over 30 seconds per Thunderdome output, don't worry about it. Just aiming for 30 seconds will make you faster.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS
Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

This Routine challenges your speed and agility across the entire skill set of LR. 

Keeping the stimulus in your working memory while independently pivoting into a new question type every 30 seconds (or less) is no easy task.

Successfully completing this Routine means you're ready for anything, no question type phases you, difficulty doesn't bother you, and you have critical intuition locked down.

How This Should Be Done

We keep the warmup light to give HIIT room to breathe.

If you've done this Routine at least once before, you can experiment with adding the answer choices on each question after you're done with all your HIIT outputs.

Answering the questions should be relatively simple if you've mastered the HIIT outputs. 

Don't overdo this Routine; don't perform it more than once every other day at maximum.

How to Move On

You don't really need to move on from this Routine since it can be useful as an intermittent check-in all the way up through test day.

sequence.name: RC Straight Through
sequence.text:
3
RC Straight Through
1 SECTION
Instructions

Translate the passage*.

Proceed to the first question and translate the question stem.

Make a Mission.

Making a Mission means answering the question yourself.

Go back to the passage to enable yourself to answer the question, if needed. Only look back at the passage in the Mission stage of the question.

Don't try to match your Mission in the answer choices.

On every individual answer choice:

Read, translate and quip the answer choice.

Investigate whether this answer choice meets the standard of what the question stem is asking.

If you think this answer meets the standard of the question stem, highlight the first word of the answer.

If you are not sure whether this answer meets the standard of the question stem, leave it open.

If you know this answer does not meets the standard of the question stem, cross it out.

Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

Hyperskip, if needed.

Aim to hyperskip a total of 5-7 questions per section.

Only go back to your hyperskips at the end of the entire section, not at the end of the passage they're associated with.

You can go back to the passage during the hyperskip.

Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

This is a great Intro RC Routine to improve question stem Translation and tone identification skills.

How This Should Be Done

Don't combine the RC Question Stem Translation Drill with the Tone Training Drill.

This Routine is intended to train the targeted skills one at a time before allowing you to put those skills to use in a Straight Through RC section.

Translate the question stems on one section, then go to a new section for your Tone Training, and another new section for your RC Straight Through. You can reuse the sections you used for RC Question Stem Translation and the Tone Training later in your prep.

After you've done your Tone Training, do RC Straight Through without the highlighting you practiced in Tone Training. Our goal is to get you to start noticing the author's tone without the highlighting, since we don't want you to be reliant on highlighting tonal indicators on test day.

I tend to not assign Tone Training for very long just because I don't want students to become overly reliant on keywords to sense the tone.

You can think of Tone Training as a step-up toward naturally feeling the author's mood in the passage, but we pair it with the RC Straight Through section so that you can put those skills into action fast without getting married to the highlighting.

How to Move On

You can move on when you no longer feel any hesitation or doubt about the author's tone and are no longer missing questions due to question stem misreads.

1
Decaf RC Translation Drill
1 PASSAGE
Instructions

NOTE: Do your recaps out loud in the beginning to keep yourself honest about the quality and completeness of the recaps. Transition to silent recaps when you feel like you're ready.

Read, translate, and quip paragraph 1*. Do it just like LR.

This means all the details are included just like they would be on LR.

Quip after every Translation. 

This standard applies to every paragraph you ever translate on RC.

Look away from paragraph 1 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 1 silently.

The recap is not a summary, gist, or main point.

The recap should not omit names, dates, and lists.

The recap should not be a shopping list of information. It should be a story in your own words.

It is encouraged to mix up the order of the sentences and ideas.

This standard applies to every paragraph (or collection of paragraphs) you ever recap on RC.

Read, translate, and quip paragraph 2. Do it just like LR.

Look away from paragraph 2 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 2 silently.

Without looking back, recap the Translations of paragraphs 1 + 2 back to back silently.

Read, translate, and quip paragraph 3. Do it just like LR.

Look away from paragraph 3 and recap the FULL TRANSLATION of paragraph 3 silently.

Without looking back, recap the Translations of paragraphs 1 + 2 + 3 back to back silently.

Repeat this pattern for all remaining paragraphs.

Complete this same process on all remaining passages in the section.

Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

This Routine can hopefully make you love RC as much as I do.

To me, there is nothing more fun than Party Tricking the questions before you read the passage. (Why can't I find a way to fit Inside Out into 35 minutes? RC would be so much better if I could figure out a way to fit Inside Out into 35 minutes!)

I know that you have to get used to Party Tricking first, but hopefully, all of your work in Modified Inside Out and Light Inside Out have demystified the RC answer choices to the point where you are ready to take on this challenge.

If you really don't want a Party Trick, you can skip the Inside Out in this Routine, but try the Spoiled Read! It's a really cool Workout that drastically decreases the intimidation you feel when you read the passage and it's 35-minute compatible.

How This Should Be Done

You're allowed to choose whatever RC Translation Drill you want for the Inside Out and the Spoiled Read. Just make sure you're still not rushing through the section.

There are a ton of RC Party Tricking resources on this platform, so I won't belabor how to Party Trick here.

But Party Tricking takes a minute to get used to; you have to learn how to be a detective when you're first getting started with it.

Don't rush the Party Trick to the point where you're just saying "I don't know" and guessing. Take it as an opportunity to learn how to play the answers against one another while you're doing it.

Watch the RC Party Tricking demos in the Loophole Online course for inspiration.

How to Move On

Hopefully we've cured your RC fear because this is the last I'm Afraid of RC Routine!

If we haven't, feel free to return to the two earlier Routines in this Routine Progression. 

Otherwise, move on to any of the I Just Want to Focus on RC Routine Progressions.

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage

What problem are we solving?

Have you ever done a section when:

  • you're falling asleep in the middle? 

  • someone else is taking a call a little too close to you? 

  • you're looking at the clock over and over again and saying to yourself "I have to speed up"?

  • you're saying to yourself, "I can't get this wrong. Oh my god, I don't understand. I have to get it. I'll never get into Berkeley. My dad is right about me."?

  • you just saw a previous score and you're going to cry?

  • you have a stye on your left eye and also maybe COVID?

Doing the LSAT like this is mental and physical self-sabotage.

You are willfully engaging in behaviors that decrease your score. 

I care about you and I care about your score, so I'm going to give you some real talk here.

Telling yourself you can't do something drastically increases the chances you won't be able to do that thing.

So stop it. 

Doing LSAT in an environment or situation that pulls on your attention sets you up to fail.

So stop it.

Thinking about the past, the future, and what other people think while you're doing the LSAT ensures that you do not do your best.

So stop it.

This is your Olympics.

We need you in peak mental and physical condition while you're training to ensure that you're in peak condition on test day. This means that you have to advocate for yourself.

Create space in your life for LSAT is to be the #1 priority, not something you do after every high priority is done.

This Accuracy Fix teaches you how to be that your advocate.

Have you ever done a section when:

you're falling asleep in the middle? 

someone else is taking a call a little too close to you? 

you're looking at the clock over and over again and saying to yourself "I have to speed up"?

you're saying to yourself, "I can't get this wrong. Oh my god, I don't understand. I have to get it. I'll never get into Berkeley. My dad is right about me."?

you just saw a previous score and you're going to cry?

you have a stye on your left eye and also maybe COVID?

Doing the LSAT like this is mental and physical self-sabotage.

You are willfully engaging in behaviors that decrease your score. 

I care about you and I care about your score, so I'm going to give you some real talk here.

Telling yourself you can't do something drastically increases the chances you won't be able to do that thing.

So stop it. 

Doing LSAT in an environment or situation that pulls on your attention sets you up to fail.

So stop it.

Thinking about the past, the future, and what other people think while you're doing the LSAT ensures that you do not do your best.

So stop it.

This is your Olympics.

We need you in peak mental and physical condition while you're training to ensure that you're in peak condition on test day. This means that you have to advocate for yourself.

Create space in your life for LSAT is to be the #1 priority, not something you do after every high priority is done.

This Accuracy Fix teaches you how to be that your advocate.

sequence.name: Time Awareness Training
sequence.text:
2
Time Awareness Training
Instructions

NOTE: Checking the time excessively during the exam is a major cause of accuracy issues. This Workout is designed to help you overcome the need to check the time by enhancing your intuitive understanding of how much time has passed.

Look at the clock and note the exact time with seconds.

Aim to look at the clock again exactly when your Time Goal has elapsed.

Five minutes is the Level 1 Time Goal, so start here on your first Time Awareness Training.

If you've done Time Awareness Training before, start at the last Time Goal you've earned.

When you think your Time Goal has elapsed, look at the clock.

You may only look at the clock once per Time Awareness Training.

If you look at the clock within one minute of your Time Goal, progress your Time Goal to the next Level tomorrow.

To progress to the next level of Time Awareness Training, you must check the clock within only one minute of your Time Goal.

If you've checked the time within one minute of the Level 5 Time Goal, congratulations! You've graduated from Time Awareness Training.

If you look at the clock farther than one minute from your Time Goal, this round of Time Awareness Training is now over.

Please restart Time Awareness Training with the same Time Goal tomorrow.
SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.name: Pacing Practice
sequence.text:
3
Pacing Practice
Instructions

Choose an interval time goal.

Your interval time goal is your target time for each question.

For example, an interval time goal may be 90 seconds per question.

Follow the procedures of How to Set a Realistic Interval Time Goal below.

Set an interval timer to repeatedly countdown from that time goal 30 times in a row.

Do not incorporate rest intervals.

We choose 30 times so we can have some extra intervals in case our timer messes up.

Start your interval timer when you begin an LR or RC section*.

For RC, only use the interval timer on the questions, not during the passage.

You must select an answer on each question before the interval timer goes off.

You cannot stay on a question longer than the interval timer permits, no matter how badly you want to.
SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

This Routine eases you into timing with minimal traumatic events. 

By doing this Routine before jumping into Test-Day Timed Sections, you enable yourself to more effectively transition your goal accuracy into a timed environment.

By studying and understanding timing on a deeper level, you train yourself to be fast as opposed to just expecting yourself to be fast.

How This Should Be Done

Gradually build up your Time Awareness Training as you progress through this Routine.

You have the option of overlapping your Time Awareness Training with other tasks as noted in the Time Awareness Training instructions, but make sure to go directly into the Cappuccino warmup and RC Pacing Practice as soon as the Time Awareness Training is completed.

This will enable you to more effectively and intuitively feel the time during your LR Pacing Practice.

How to Move On

You can move on from this Routine when you no longer feel the urge to check the clock to know how much time has passed.

I want you to trust yourself and your own internal clock so that you don't distract yourself on test day.

Stop Mental and Physical Self-Sabotage
What Problem Are We Solving?

Have you ever done a section when:

you're falling asleep in the middle? 

someone else is taking a call a little too close to you? 

you're looking at the clock over and over again and saying to yourself "I have to speed up"?

you're saying to yourself, "I can't get this wrong. Oh my god, I don't understand. I have to get it. I'll never get into Berkeley. My dad is right about me."?

you just saw a previous score and you're going to cry?

you have a stye on your left eye and also maybe COVID?

Doing the LSAT like this is mental and physical self-sabotage.

You are willfully engaging in behaviors that decrease your score. 

I care about you and I care about your score, so I'm going to give you some real talk here.

Telling yourself you can't do something drastically increases the chances you won't be able to do that thing.

So stop it. 

Doing LSAT in an environment or situation that pulls on your attention sets you up to fail.

So stop it.

Thinking about the past, the future, and what other people think while you're doing the LSAT ensures that you do not do your best.

So stop it.

This is your Olympics.

We need you in peak mental and physical condition while you're training to ensure that you're in peak condition on test day. This means that you have to advocate for yourself.

Create space in your life for LSAT is to be the #1 priority, not something you do after every high priority is done.

This Accuracy Fix teaches you how to be that your advocate.

You engage in non-productive self-talk during and after section practice
You rush through questions you find intimidating
You train when you're low on food, sleep, and emotional fortitude
You catastrophize mistakes to the point where every error makes you worse at the test ("This proves I can't do law school")
Your section scores are significantly better than PT and test-day scores

Write In
Instructions

NOTE: The Write In replaces the Mission step of the Full LR Process.

Read and translate the stimulus in chunks*. 

Quip each chunk of the stimulus after you translate.

Continue until the end of the stimulus.

Mark the conclusion.

Immediately proceed to the CLIR after your final quip of the stimulus (or the final quip is the CLIR).

Read the question stem, identify the question type and whether the question is Powerful-Provable.

Write in a correct answer to the question.

Make the Write In answer sound like a real answer choice, not a messy note.

On every individual answer choice:

Read, translate, and quip the answer choice.

Investigate whether this answer choice meets the question type's Back Up Plan.

If you think this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, highlight the first word of the answer.

If you are not sure whether this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, leave it open.

If you know this answer doesn't meet the Back-Up Plan question, cross it out.

Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

Hyperskip, if needed.

Aim to hyperskip 5-7 questions per section.

Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS
Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

This Routine exists to force students to refine their autonomous thinking when it comes to LR answer choices.

If you're overly reliant on the answer choices to suggest at you, you'll always be at their mercy. 

The Thunderdome multiplies every stimulus into almost every question type and doesn't give you any answer choices to suggest any correct outcomes. This is a great Routine for finding out where you have trouble thinking for yourself and then reviewing accordingly. 

But then, by moving directly into a Write In, we get to take our Thunderdome skills and actualize them into a real question-answering section immediately and see how we do with a score (which we'll only find out after Camoing the next day or at the end of the week, right? 😉😉).

How This Should Be Done

You can customize how long you spend on the Thunderdome before going into the Write In.

Ideally, you'll have time to do a full section of Thunderdoming. But given that Thunderdoming can take a fair amount of time, especially when you haven't done many before, you might want to cap your Thunderdome at 1 hour and then move directly into your Write In.

For the Write In, use natural pace timing, but keep adrenaline in your veins.

How to Move On

When your Write Ins directly overlap with the correct answer more often than not and you don't have any remaining hesitation with any of your Thunderdome outputs, you can progress to a new Advanced routine. (Perhaps integrating a HIIT into the mix?)

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Don't Be Desperate in the Answers
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Don't Be Desperate in the Answers

What problem are we solving?

Sometimes you just want to get the question right so badly that every answer choice looks like an escape hatch.

"Is it right? Is it right!??

If it's right, then I can move on.

Then I won't waste any more time.

Then the stimulus must have meant this.

Then this must have been what they were looking for."

Notice the desperation dripping off this monologue. 

You're looking for an answer choice to rescue you, but actually the roles need to be reversed. You have to be the strong one.

Be for real. You are better than 80% wrong. 

Answer choices are designed to exploit your desire for them to be right and to prey on moments of inattention.

sequence.name: Masterpiece
sequence.text:
2
Masterpiece
Instructions

NOTE: Masterpieces are multi-day workouts focused on a single section*. You can do a three-day Masterpiece or a four-day Masterpiece to start. Don't worry, you do less and less work as the Masterpiece progresses each day.

Complete the section in any workout style.

Mark questions for hyperskip, but don't perform your hyperskip pass yet.

When you're done with the section, put it aside without grading it.

The next day, redo each question in the section fully.

When you return to the section, keep your answer selected at first, but uncross off all other answer choices.

Do not just look at your previous answer without actually redoing the full question. Your objective is to decide whether you want to stick to your previous answer or choose a new answer.

On each question you have three options:

Lock in your previous answer.

Once an answer is locked, you will not look at this question again until Camo Day. Locking is a way to signal to yourself that you know this answer is correct and do not need to look at it again.

Do not lock in more than 50% of your remaining answers on any lock-in pass until you get to the last day of your Masterpiece.

Keep your answer the same, but leave the question unlocked.

Leave a question unlocked if you are not sure about whether the answer you've selected is correct.

Change your answer.

If you change your answer, you may not lock the question on this pass.

The next day, return only to your unlocked questions and redo them. Decide to lock in or change your answers, following the same procedure you did on day 2.

This process repeats for however many days your Masterpiece will last.

Make sure all questions are locked in by the last day.

Optional: On the last day, print out a fresh copy of the section and redo it straight-through.

Compare the fresh section to your locked-in answers and see if there are any differences. If so, reconcile the two sections. Decide on your final answer before putting it into Camo.

After your last pass on the section, with all answers locked in, proceed with Camo and Wrong Answer Journaling.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.name: Method/Flaw/Argument Part Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet
sequence.text:
3
Method/Flaw/Argument Part Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet
Instructions

Make a spreadsheet with three columns, or use this template:

Column 1: Vexing Answer Choice

Column 2: Answer Choice Translation

Column 3: Corresponding Stimulus

Collect all the difficult answer choices to translate, focusing especially on Method/Flaw/Argument Part answer choices.

If nothing seems to improve your score, this Routine is for you.

Since the Masterpiece takes different amounts of time on different days, you can contract or extend the Method/Flaw/Argument Part Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet time to fill your study block.

For example, if you're on the third day of your Masterpiece and you don't have that many questions to complete, use that time as an opportunity to dive more deeply into your Method/Flaw/Argument Part Answer Choice Translation Spreadsheet.

You can also layer this Routine with a second Masterpiece section on a staggered start day. This means you would begin another Masterpiece section on day 2 or 3 of the first section's Masterpiece. This would allow you to get more Masterpiece sections done throughout the week and potentially see a lot more improvement.

Move on from this Routine when your accuracy improves.

sequence.text:
2
Masterpiece
Instructions

NOTE: Masterpieces are multi-day workouts focused on a single section*. You can do a three-day Masterpiece or a four-day Masterpiece to start. Don't worry, you do less and less work as the Masterpiece progresses each day.

Complete the section in any workout style.

Mark questions for hyperskip, but don't perform your hyperskip pass yet.

When you're done with the section, put it aside without grading it.

The next day, redo each question in the section fully.

When you return to the section, keep your answer selected at first, but uncross off all other answer choices.

Do not just look at your previous answer without actually redoing the full question. Your objective is to decide whether you want to stick to your previous answer or choose a new answer.

On each question you have three options:

Lock in your previous answer.

Once an answer is locked, you will not look at this question again until Camo Day. Locking is a way to signal to yourself that you know this answer is correct and do not need to look at it again.

Do not lock in more than 50% of your remaining answers on any lock-in pass until you get to the last day of your Masterpiece.

Keep your answer the same, but leave the question unlocked.

Leave a question unlocked if you are not sure about whether the answer you've selected is correct.

Change your answer.

If you change your answer, you may not lock the question on this pass.

The next day, return only to your unlocked questions and redo them. Decide to lock in or change your answers, following the same procedure you did on day 2.

This process repeats for however many days your Masterpiece will last.

Make sure all questions are locked in by the last day.

Optional: On the last day, print out a fresh copy of the section and redo it straight-through.

Compare the fresh section to your locked-in answers and see if there are any differences. If so, reconcile the two sections. Decide on your final answer before putting it into Camo.

After your last pass on the section, with all answers locked in, proceed with Camo and Wrong Answer Journaling.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

inline_prep.html:
Accuracy
Intuition, Not Impulse
  1. Prep Map/
  2. Accuracy

Intuition, Not Impulse

What problem are we solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

FIX 1 OF 7
Intuition, Not Impulse
What Problem Are We Solving?

Impulse is great until you have no idea why you chose a wrong answer.

Acting on impulse is like the evil twin of acting on intuition. It happens when you try to be fast before you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level.

Intuition takes over after you've ingrained the process at a subconscious level. Intuition can be reliable and purposeful. 

Impulse can't. 

I know you think I don't understand: "Like come on, Ellen. Don't you know I have to do this in 35 minutes?" I get you.

This advice is coming from someone who could -0 Logical Reasoning sections in 27 minutes one month after meeting the LSAT for the first time.

It's not that I love to be slow or want you to be slow; I actually love speed. My Spotify history of Eminem's Rap God has the receipts (yes that song is so problematic it's also so fast and it just soothes my brain so much).

But I want you to be right more than I want you to be fast. If you're right, you can train to be fast. If you're fast and wrong, you'll have to slow down to train to be right.

No matter how quickly or intuitively I ever choose an answer, if you were to freeze time and say, "Hey Ellen, why'd you do that?" I'd be able to tell you.

Even if I'm not consciously thinking out all the words behind my decision, I could tell you why I'm doing it. If you can't say why you're doing something, it creates score variation, the hallmark of acting on impulse rather than purpose.

There will be a time when you'll approach the LSAT intuitively, but that intuition will be rooted in strategy. This Accuracy Fix is meant to ingrain that reliable, process-driven strategy that will mature into intuition.

You take care of the process, and the process will take care of the test.

sequence.name: Question Stem Training
sequence.text:
2
Question Stem Training
Instructions

Identify all the LR question stem types and their associated Back Up Plans in a section*.

For instance, after reading a Weaken question stem, say, "Weaken. Does this make the conclusion less likely to be true?"

Do not look at the stimulus or answer choices.

This is not the time to attempt to answer the question.

Go to the LSAT Question Database to check your question stem identifications.

On the stems you get wrong, write down(on your scratch paper or using this template):

The exact text of the stem you misidentified

Your wrong question stem identification

The correct question stem identification

How you could know the correct identification next time

Review the stems you misidentified and how you could identify them correctly before every Question Stem Training workout.

Only stop Question Stem Training once you can reliably hit 100% question type and Back Up Plan identification accuracy on three sections in a row.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.name: LR Straight Through
sequence.text:
3
LR Straight Through
1 SECTION
Instructions

Read and translate the stimulus in chunks*. 

Quip each chunk of the stimulus after you translate.

Continue until the end of the stimulus.

Mark the conclusion.

Immediately proceed to the CLIR after your final quip of the stimulus (or the final quip is the CLIR).

Read the question stem, identify the question type and whether the question is Powerful-Provable.

Make a Mission.

Making a Mission means answering the question yourself, except on Strengthen and Weaken questions. On these questions, your Mission should be a stimulus-specific goal for the answer choice to hit.

You are allowed to go back to the stimulus when you make a Mission.

Don't try to match your Mission in the answer choices.

On every individual answer choice:

Read, translate, and quip the answer choice.

Investigate whether this answer choice meets the question type's Back Up Plan.

If you think this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, highlight the first word of the answer.

If you are not sure whether this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, leave it open.

If you know this answer doesn't meet the Back-Up Plan question, cross it out.

Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

Hyperskip, if needed.

Aim to hyperskip 5-7 questions per section.

Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

3

LR Straight Through

1 section

Instructions

  1. Read and translate the stimulus in chunks*. 

  2. Quip each chunk of the stimulus after you translate.

  3. Continue until the end of the stimulus.

  4. Mark the conclusion.

  5. Immediately proceed to the CLIR after your final quip of the stimulus (or the final quip is the CLIR).

  6. Read the question stem, identify the question type and whether the question is Powerful-Provable.

  7. Make a Mission.

    1. Making a Mission means answering the question yourself, except on Strengthen and Weaken questions. On these questions, your Mission should be a stimulus-specific goal for the answer choice to hit.

    2. You are allowed to go back to the stimulus when you make a Mission.

    3. Don't try to match your Mission in the answer choices.

  8. On every individual answer choice:

    1. Read, translate, and quip the answer choice.

    2. Investigate whether this answer choice meets the question type's Back Up Plan.

      1. If you think this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, highlight the first word of the answer.

      2. If you are not sure whether this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, leave it open.

      3. If you know this answer doesn't meet the Back-Up Plan question, cross it out.

  9. Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

  10. Hyperskip, if needed.

    1. Aim to hyperskip 5-7 questions per section.

  11. Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

sequence.name: Camo Review
sequence.text:
5
Camo Review
Instructions

When you finish an LR or RC section in LawHub, do not press Complete Section. Instead, write down your answers.

Use Self-Paced Mode on all LR and RC sections. Never use Exam Mode.

At least 24 hours later, enter your answers into Camo Review.

Do not check your answers against the answer key before entering your answers into Camo Review.

Camo Review will give you a list of questions to return to.

This list includes all of your wrong answers and an unknown number of decoy correct answers.

Reattempt all of the questions in your Camo Review from scratch. Attempt to do a better job on the question now than you did the first time.

Doing a better job means you should retranslate, requip, and re-CLIR the stimulus on LR or retranslate and requip the passage on RC. Retranslate every part of the question, consider every answer choice, and try to correct your process mistakes before choosing a new answer.

Enter all your new answers into Camo Review.

Camo Review will identify all your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, Self-Doubt, and Self-Confidence answers.

Your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, and Self-Doubt answers have been automatically added to your Wrong Answer Journal. Go to your Wrong Answer Journal now to immediately begin the Wrong Answer Journal process.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

sequence.name: Wrong Answer Journal
sequence.text:
6
Wrong Answer Journal
Instructions

After you've Camoed your LR or RC section, begin the Wrong Answer Journaling process.

For each wrong answer, fill in the date you did the section, the question number that was wrong, and the answer you chose.

This information will already be filled in for you if you Camo using Loophole Online.

Fill in your Reason Missed column

In this column, write down what you did wrong that caused you to miss this question.

Ask yourself, "Why did I think that this wrong answer was right? Why did I think that this right answer was wrong?" Focus on changing the actions that enabled these mistaken judgments.

The first word of every entry in this column should be "I." 

Example: "I misidentified the question stem."

This will force you to reflect on what you did that caused you to choose the wrong answer and overlook the right answer.

Fill in your Solution column

In this column, write down what you will do differently to ensure you don't make this same mistake again.

Ask yourself, "What could I have done that would have made me realize in the moment that the wrong answer is wrong? What could I have done that would have made me realize in the moment that the right answer is right?"

The first words of every entry in this column should be "I will..." 

Example: "I will do Question Stem Training to improve my ability to correctly identify question types."

Frame your Solution Column as a direct response to the Reason Missed column.

Click here to go to your Wrong Answer Journal

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS

Example: "I misidentified the question stem."

This will force you to reflect on what you did that caused you to choose the wrong answer and overlook the right answer.

Fill in your Solution column

In this column, write down what you will do differently to ensure you don't make this same mistake again.

Ask yourself, "What could I have done that would have made me realize in the moment that the wrong answer is wrong? What could I have done that would have made me realize in the moment that the right answer is right?"

The first words of every entry in this column should be "I will..." 

Example: "I will do Question Stem Training to improve my ability to correctly identify question types."

Frame your Solution Column as a direct response to the Reason Missed column.

Click here to go to your Wrong Answer Journal

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS
Ellen's Advice
Why Are We Doing This?

This Routine serves as a light basic introduction to LR accuracy. 

It allows you to review some objectives from the Learn and Translation Prep Stages, while solidifying your question stem identifications and making sure you're solid on Method vocab.

But this Routine will still push you forward with LR full sections to iron out your LR Full Question Process and gradually improve your performance through review.

How This Should Be Done

Make sure you do this Routine exactly in the order provided.

Don't skip the Translation warmup and don't put the Question Stem Training any later in the Routine.

It's important to do Question Stem Training right before your LR Straight Through Section because we want to reinforce accurate question stem identification in that full section.

How to Move On

Once you beat Question Stem Training and the Method Vocab Remix, you can graduate from this Routine to the other Accuracy Fix Routines.

sequence.name: LR Straight Through
sequence.text:
3
LR Straight Through
1 SECTION
Instructions

Read and translate the stimulus in chunks*. 

Quip each chunk of the stimulus after you translate.

Continue until the end of the stimulus.

Mark the conclusion.

Immediately proceed to the CLIR after your final quip of the stimulus (or the final quip is the CLIR).

Read the question stem, identify the question type and whether the question is Powerful-Provable.

Make a Mission.

Making a Mission means answering the question yourself, except on Strengthen and Weaken questions. On these questions, your Mission should be a stimulus-specific goal for the answer choice to hit.

You are allowed to go back to the stimulus when you make a Mission.

Don't try to match your Mission in the answer choices.

On every individual answer choice:

Read, translate, and quip the answer choice.

Investigate whether this answer choice meets the question type's Back Up Plan.

If you think this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, highlight the first word of the answer.

If you are not sure whether this answer meets the Back-Up Plan question, leave it open.

If you know this answer doesn't meet the Back-Up Plan question, cross it out.

Choose amongst the open and highlighted answer choices.

Hyperskip, if needed.

Aim to hyperskip 5-7 questions per section.

Use any remaining time to return to your hyperskips.

sequence.name: Camo Review
sequence.text:
5
Camo Review
Instructions

When you finish an LR or RC section in LawHub, do not press Complete Section. Instead, write down your answers.

Use Self-Paced Mode on all LR and RC sections. Never use Exam Mode.

At least 24 hours later, enter your answers into Camo Review.

Do not check your answers against the answer key before entering your answers into Camo Review.

Camo Review will give you a list of questions to return to.

This list includes all of your wrong answers and an unknown number of decoy correct answers.

Reattempt all of the questions in your Camo Review from scratch. Attempt to do a better job on the question now than you did the first time.

Doing a better job means you should retranslate, requip, and re-CLIR the stimulus on LR or retranslate and requip the passage on RC. Retranslate every part of the question, consider every answer choice, and try to correct your process mistakes before choosing a new answer.

Enter all your new answers into Camo Review.

Camo Review will identify all your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, Self-Doubt, and Self-Confidence answers.

Your Misreads, Conceptual Gaps, and Self-Doubt answers have been automatically added to your Wrong Answer Journal. Go to your Wrong Answer Journal now to immediately begin the Wrong Answer Journal process.

SEE FULL WORKOUT DETAILS
